title: How do you securely handle refresh tokens and revocation?
description: Short-lived access tokens, rotation with reuse detection, storage locations, and logout semantics.

data.text: **Question:** How do you securely handle refresh tokens and revocation?

Issue a **short-lived access token** (minutes) that the API trusts statelessly, plus a **long-lived refresh token** used only at the authorization server to obtain a new pair. On every use, **rotate** the refresh token — and if an old, already-rotated token ever reappears, treat it as stolen: revoke the whole token family. Access tokens stay in memory on the client; refresh tokens live in HttpOnly cookies (web) or secure platform storage (mobile), never in `localStorage`.

**Why two tokens:**
- Short access-token lifetime limits the damage of a stolen token — there is no global revocation list for stateless JWTs, so *expiry is your revocation*
- Long refresh-token lifetime keeps users signed in without re-authentication
- The refresh token is only ever sent to the token endpoint — never to resource APIs

**Rotation and reuse detection:**
- Each refresh issues a new access token **and** a new refresh token; the old one is invalidated
- Track token **families** (session lineage): if a rotated-out token is presented again, the family is presumed compromised → revoke every token in the family and force re-authentication
- Rotation also protects against refresh tokens that are replayed after logout

**Storage and transport:**
- Web SPA: refresh token in an **HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite** cookie scoped to the auth server, with CSRF protection on the refresh endpoint; access token in memory only
- Mobile/native: platform secure storage (Keychain / Keystore) with biometric unlock where appropriate
- Never persist tokens in `localStorage` — any XSS reads them wholesale
- **Logout/revocation:** record revoked refresh tokens (or session ids) server-side and check on refresh; access tokens die naturally within their short TTL — optionally pair with a short-lived denylist for immediate kill
- Absolute expiration: even valid sessions end after N days — force re-authentication

data.title: Rotation with family reuse detection

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Why stateless JWTs need short lifetimes (no instant revocation)
- Rotation semantics and reuse detection — the security core of the pattern
- Correct client storage per platform, and why localStorage is wrong
- Real logout: server-side revocation, not just deleting client state

items: Access tokens that live for hours or days — 'revocation' becomes impossible
Storing refresh tokens in localStorage or IndexedDB where any XSS exfiltrates them
Not rotating: the same refresh token works forever once stolen
Deleting tokens client-side and calling it logout while the server still honors them
Unbounded refresh chains with no absolute expiry or session timeout
Concurrent refreshes invalidating each other in multi-tab apps — deduplicate the flow
A JWT is valid but the user was just fired — how do you deny them immediately?
How do you handle refresh in a SPA with four open tabs?
Where should the refresh token live in a browser, and why not the Authorization header?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Short-lived access tokens + long-lived, rotating refresh tokens
Reuse of a rotated token revokes the whole family
Web: refresh in HttpOnly cookie; access token in memory; never localStorage
Logout must revoke server-side state, not just clear the client
data.takeaway: Limit exposure with short access tokens, rotate refresh tokens with reuse detection, and store them where scripts can't reach.
